certainty_reasoning: The sexual allegation exists only in Queensberry's plea (10 St James's Place, October 1893 - April 1894). Scarfe never testified and no indictment count concerned him. What the trial record documents on oath: Taylor introduced Scarfe to Wilde at St James's Place, Scarfe called there five or six times (the waiter Price), dined alone with Wilde, received a £4 cigarette case, and last dined with Wilde at the Avondale Hotel in February 1895; Wilde swore he 'never embraced, kissed or caressed him.' Plea-only → 'alleged' with disputed block.
summary: Ernest Scarfe, a young valet-turned-clerk who had been to the Australian gold-diggings — meeting Lord Douglas of Hawick on the voyage out in 1893 — knew Taylor from the Knightsbridge Skating Rink and was introduced by him to Wilde at 10 St James's Place. He visited repeatedly, dined alone with Wilde, and received the customary cigarette case; the acquaintance ran to a dinner at the Avondale in February 1895. Queensberry's plea alleged solicitation and gross indecency at St James's Place; Scarfe was never called and the allegation never charged.

disputed.claim: that Wilde solicited Ernest Scarfe to commit sodomy and committed acts of gross indecency with him at 10 St James's Place between October 1893 and April 1894
disputed.disputed_by: Wilde's sworn denial at the libel trial ('I have never embraced, kissed or caressed him')
disputed.grounds: allegation stands in the plea alone: no indictment count concerned Scarfe and he gave no evidence at any of the three proceedings in Hyde's record

sources.quote: You knew a man named Ernest Scarfe?—Yes. He was introduced to me by Taylor. He is a young man of about twenty, of no occupation. He had been in Australia at the gold-diggings. … I asked Scarfe to dine with myself and Taylor at Kettner's. I did not afterwards take him back to my rooms at St. James's. I have never embraced, kissed or caressed him. … Did you give him any presents?—Yes, a cigarette case. It cost £4. It is my custom to present cigarette cases. I last saw Scarfe in February when he dined with me at the Avondale Hotel.
sources.context: Wilde's cross-examination by Carson, Regina (Wilde) v. Queensberry, April 1895
sources.supports: the acquaintance's shape on Wilde's oath: Taylor's introduction, dinners, the cigarette case, the February 1895 Avondale dinner, and the denial of physical contact

sources.quote: CARSON: Did you ever kiss him? WILDE: Never in my life. CARSON: Or caress him in any way? WILDE: No. CARSON: Or attempt to have indecencies with him? WILDE: Never in my life. CARSON: Why did you ask him to dinner? WILDE: Because I am very good-natured, because it is one of the best ways perhaps of pleasing anybody, particularly anyone not in one's social position, to ask him to dine. (Laughter.)
sources.context: Carson's cross-examination on Ernest Scarfe, Thursday morning 4 April 1895. Compare Hyde 1948 p. 149, which reduces the three-question sequence to 'I have never embraced, kissed or caressed him' and omits the class answer and the court's laughter entirely.
